plan.topic_summary: OLED displays are a core component in XR headsets, where brightness, power efficiency, and pixel density directly determine user experience and device form factor. Over the next 1–5 years, the trajectory of OLED (and micro-OLED) technology will shape whether current XR hardware can evolve toward lighter, brighter, more power-efficient devices or whether alternative display technologies will displace it.
key_questions: What are the current brightness, efficiency, and PPI benchmarks for OLED panels in shipping XR devices, and how do they compare to the thresholds needed for comfortable outdoor AR use?
How is the transition from micro-OLED toward next-generation display technologies (e.g., microLED) progressing in the XR supply chain, and what timeline is realistic for displacement?
How are OLED panel costs trending for XR-specific form factors, and what does this imply for device pricing and volume ramp?
What are the key reliability and lifetime concerns (burn-in, degradation, thermal stress) that could limit OLED adoption in always-on or high-brightness XR use cases?
How does display quality (brightness, color accuracy, PPI) correlate with content adoption and consumer retention in XR ecosystems over a 3–5 year horizon?

sources.title: Perspective: OLED Displays Singing with the Blues
sources.abstract: While blue pixels consume approximately 50% of the energy of organic light-emitting diode (OLED) display front planes, in the 25 years since their invention, 100% internal efficiency phosphorescent OLEDs (PHOLEDs) have not met the stability standards necessary for their adoption. In this perspective, we discuss the significant progress and challenges encountered during this long journey of exploration and discovery. Today, using a combination of solutions including robust molecular design, graded doping of the emission layer, increasing the optical density of states to decrease the triplet radiative lifetime, and employing light outcoupling schemes, deep blue PHOLEDs are now achieving lifetimes approaching those of their green analogs. This perspective elaborates on the challenges and opportunities confronting further development of triplet-controlled emitters, including PHOLEDs using heavy-metal phosphors and thermally activated delayed fluorescent OLEDs. We also address some persistent problems commonly found in the literature concerning the measurement of quantum efficiency and operational lifetime.

sources.title: Physics-Constrained Graph Neural Networks for Spatio-Temporal Prediction of Drop Impact on OLED Display Panels
sources.abstract: This study aims to predict the spatio-temporal evolution of physical quantities observed in multi-layered display panels subjected to the drop impact of a ball. To model these complex interactions, graph neural networks have emerged as promising tools, effectively representing objects and their relationships as graph structures. In particular, MeshGraphNets (MGNs) excel in capturing dynamics in dynamic physics simulations using irregular mesh data. However, conventional MGNs often suffer from non-physical artifacts, such as the penetration of overlapping objects. To resolve this, we propose a physics-constrained MGN that mitigates these penetration issues while maintaining high level of accuracy in temporal predictions. Furthermore, to enhance the model's robustness, we explore noise injection strategies with varying magnitudes and different combinations of targeted components, such as the ball, the plate, or both. In addition, our analysis on model stability in spatio-temporal predictions reveals that during the inference, deriving next time-step node positions by predicting relative changes (e.g., displacement or velocity) between the current and future states yields superior accuracy compared to direct absolute position predictions. This approach consistently shows greater stability and reliability in determining subsequent node positions across various scenarios. Building on this validated model, we evaluate its generalization performance by examining its ability to extrapolate with respect to design variables. Furthermore, the physics-constrained MGN serves as a near real-time emulator for the design optimization of multi-layered OLED display panels, where thickness variables are optimized to minimize stress in the light-emitting materials. It outperforms conventional MGN in optimization tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness for practical design applications.

sources.title: The Steady Evolution of OLED Displays
sources.abstract: Abstract OLED's flexibility has made it the dominant display technology in premium smartphones. As the technology continues to improve, it is gaining traction in the automotive, IT, and AR/VR markets.

sources.title: ReHome Earth: A VR-Based Concept Validation for AI-Driven Space Homesickness Interventions
sources.abstract: Space exploration has advanced rapidly, but the emotional needs of astronauts on long-duration missions remain underexplored. We present ReHome Earth, a dual-component design approach addressing space homesickness: 1) a future-oriented installation concept integrating transparent OLED displays with spaceship windows for real-time Earth connectivity, and 2) a functional VR prototype simulating astronaut isolation for testing AI-generated content effectiveness. Since accessing astronauts during missions is impossible, we conducted concept validation with terrestrial participants experiencing geographic displacement. Through evaluation with 84 proxy participants and 6 HCI experts, we demonstrate strong emotional resonance and validate three design implications: emotional pacing mechanisms, explainable biophysical feedback systems, and evolution from individual tools to collective affective infrastructure. Our contributions include a technically feasible space installation concept, a functional VR prototype for space HCI research, and empirical insights into the design of AI-driven emotional support systems for extreme isolation environments.

sources.title: Color Calibration Methods For OLED Displays
sources.abstract: Accurate color reproduction on a display requires an inverse display model, mapping colorimetric values (e.g. CIE XYZ) into RGB values driving the display. To create such a model, we collected a large dataset of display color measurements for a high refresh-rate 4-primary OLED display. We demonstrated that, unlike traditional LCD displays, multi-primary OLED display color responses are non-additive and non-linear for some colors. We tested the performances of different regression methods: polynomial regression, look-up tables, multi-layer perceptrons, and others. The best-performing models were additionally validated on newly measured (unseen) test colors. We found that the performances of several variations of 4th-degree polynomial models were comparable to the look-up table and machine-learning-based models while being less resource-intensive.

sources.title: Treat-through OLED Displays: Dosimetry and performance of OLED AVATAR screens for Megavoltage Radiotherapy
sources.abstract: The AVATAR system utilizes a radiolucent video display to help relax and immobilize pediatric patients during radiotherapy. This study investigates the use of OLED (Organic Light Emitting Diode) displays, which offer superior image quality and faster alignment compared to traditional projector-based systems, albeit with slightly increased thickness. The dose perturbations caused by these screens were assessed to evaluate their suitability for radiotherapy. A 20 cm OLED screen was positioned in the patient's line of sight, between the patient's head and the radiation source. The screen comprises a 0.25 mm thick flexible OLED panel and a custom carbon fiber backing (0.3 to 0.6 mm thick), with most electronic components relocated via ribbon cable. 6 MV portal images were captured with and without the screen to create transmission maps. Additionally, parallel plate ion chamber measurements were taken at the surface and at depth in a solid water phantom. The OLED's radiation tolerance was tested with a 100 Gy dose delivery and 12 months of use in an active radiotherapy linac vault. The portal image transmission maps indicated an average attenuation difference of 0.3\% (SD = 0.37 \%) between measurements with and without the AVATAR screen, with a maximum point attenuation of 3\%. Ion chamber measurements revealed a 0.31\% decrease in dose at 2 cm depth and a 7.04 \% increase at the surface under an anterior-posterior beam. For a VMAT arc, the dose difference was 0.04 \% at 2 cm depth and 0.1\% at the phantom surface. The minimal dose deviations indicate that these screens are suitable for megavoltage arc therapy without significantly affecting the target dose. While surface dose is slightly increased for static anterior beams, it remains low. For lower photon energies or particle beams, larger perturbations may occur, necessitating further measurements or beam entry avoidance.

sources.title: MAX OLED Solution for Next‐Generation OLED Displays
sources.abstract: Abstract A breakthrough in OLED display pixel architecture and manufacturing technology will enhance display performance and enable a wider range of applications.

sources.title: CosmicWatch: The Desktop Muon Detector(v3X)
sources.abstract: The CosmicWatch Desktop Muon Detector (v3X) is a compact, low-cost, and portable device designed for detecting ionizing radiation, including cosmic-ray muons. Building on previous iterations, the v3X introduces significant hardware and firmware improvements that enhance sensitivity, usability, and data acquisition capabilities. The detector integrates a plastic scintillator and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), custom designed electronics for signal processing, onboard data storage, OLED display, environmental sensors, and USB connectivity. With a total component cost under \$100 and a build time suitable for high school students, the v3X is ideal for education, outreach, and introductory research applications in particle and astroparticle physics. This paper details the design, performance, and potential use cases of the v3X, supported by example measurements demonstrating its functionality.

sources.title: The application of organic materials used in OLED display
sources.abstract: Based on the advantages of higher luminous efficiency, lower energy consumption and ecological protection, the organic light-emitting diode (OLED) has become a new type of display in mobile OLED device, which was also called as the dream display. Many organic materials including polyimide (PI), photoresist (PR), photosensitive polyimide (PSPI), OLED emissive layer materials, inkjet printing (IJP), optical clear adhesive (OCA) and undercut pixel definition layer (undercut PDL) have been introduced during the manufacturing process of OLED display. The pol less progress (PLP) technology had also been introduced in the OLED display by replacing the polarizer, which also introduced a few new organic materials such as black pixel definition layer (BPDL), black matrix (BM) and color film (CF) and applied in the OLED display. In this paper, the author had a review on the organic materials used in the manufacturing process of an OLED display, which included the application of organic materials used in the array structure, the emissive layer (EL) structure, the display of things (DOT) structure and the new OLED display based on the PLP technology. The application of organic material undercut PDL which was used for forming the protruding spacing columns between pixels to prevent the lateral leakage of current between adjacent pixels was also described detailed in this paper.

sources.title: Modeling and Exploiting the Time Course of Chromatic Adaptation for Display Power Optimizations in Virtual Reality
sources.abstract: We introduce a gaze-tracking--free method to reduce OLED display power consumption in VR with minimal perceptual impact. This technique exploits the time course of chromatic adaptation, the human visual system's ability to maintain stable color perception under changing illumination. To that end, we propose a novel psychophysical paradigm that models how human adaptation state changes with the scene illuminant. We exploit this model to compute an optimal illuminant shift trajectory, controlling the rate and extent of illumination change, to reduce display power under a given perceptual loss budget. Our technique significantly improves the perceptual quality over prior work that applies illumination shifts instantaneously. Our technique can also be combined with prior work on luminance dimming to reduce display power by 31% with no statistical loss of perceptual quality.

sources.title: The Design of a Detection Robot with OLED Display
sources.abstract: OLED display has the advantages of self-illumination, wide viewing angle, fast response, small size, small weight, flexibility. It is a huge breakthrough in the field of display technology, and enhances the visual enjoyment and on-the-spot experience of people. With the rapid development of science and technology, the combination of OLED and robot has attracted attention from most of the fields. In this paper, the working principle, advantages and main application fields of OLED devices are introduced, and a detection robot with OLED is designed. The detection robot can accurately control the speed of the motor and the angle of the steering gear within a distance of 1,000 meters, and receive the images from airborne cameras in real time.

sources.title: IoT-Enabled Smart Car Parking System through Integrated Sensors and Mobile Applications
sources.abstract: Due to more population congestion and car ownership, the provision of parking spaces for vehicles is becoming a crucial factor. This paper aims to present a novel Internet of Things (IoT)--based smart car parking system that can effectively manage these problems with the help of sensor technology and automation. Infrared (IR) sensors, DHT22 sensors, MQ-2 gas sensors, and servo motors are used in the parking space. An OLED display shows the status of parking slots in real-time. Communicating with a mobile application through the Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) protocol enables the efficient exchange of data. As a result, this innovative solution optimizes parking space, increases efficiency, and makes the parking lot more comfortable. This IoT system allows real-time monitoring and automation of parked cars as well as fast response to dynamic changes in environmental conditions, setting a new standard for smart parking systems.

sources.title: OLED lifetime simulation for VR displays
sources.abstract: This paper introduces a new methodology for simulating the burn-in of an organic light-emitting diode (OLED) microdisplay used in a virtual reality (VR) headset. The proposed simulation employs the stretched exponential decay (SED) model, which is widely used to predict the degradation of the OLED device over time. Furthermore, the model integrates the impact of user head motion on VR display image content. The study defines productivity and gaming mode surrogate image content from which to simulate burn-in and applies image processing correlating to head motion data collected from a user study. The results of this study indicate that head motion has a significant impact on OLED burn-in. Given a conservative assumption for image content and head motion, the time for visual failure due to burn-in artifacts is 4 times slower than a case with stationary image content.

sources.title: Solution-processed OLEDs for printing displays
sources.abstract: Recent advances in solution-processed organic light-emitting diodes toward printing displays are reviewed in terms of light-emitting materials, devices, printing techniques and applications.

sources.title: Electrically driven organic laser using integrated OLED pumping
sources.abstract: Abstract Organic semiconductors are carbon-based materials that combine optoelectronic properties with simple fabrication and the scope for tuning by changing their chemical structure1–3. They have been successfully used to make organic light-emitting diodes2,4,5 (OLEDs, now widely found in mobile phone displays and televisions), solar cells1, transistors6 and sensors7. However, making electrically driven organic semiconductor lasers is very challenging8,9. It is difficult because organic semiconductors typically support only low current densities, suffer substantial absorption from injected charges and triplets, and have additional losses due to contacts10,11. In short, injecting charges into the gain medium leads to intolerable losses. Here we take an alternative approach in which charge injection and lasing are spatially separated, thereby greatly reducing losses. We achieve this by developing an integrated device structure that efficiently couples an OLED, with exceptionally high internal-light generation, with a polymer distributed feedback laser. Under the electrical driving of the integrated structure, we observe a threshold in light output versus drive current, with a narrow emission spectrum and the formation of a beam above the threshold. These observations confirm lasing. Our results provide an organic electronic device that has not been previously demonstrated, and show that indirect electrical pumping by an OLED is a very effective way of realizing an electrically driven organic semiconductor laser. This provides an approach to visible lasers that could see applications in spectroscopy, metrology and sensing.

sources.title: P‐14.14: IJP OLEDs Advanced Adaptive De‐burn‐in algorithm
sources.venue: SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers
sources.abstract: We propose a solution to IS (Image Sticking), one of the important issue in IJPOLEDs , which has various advantages over conventional vacuum deposition methods. One solution to IS is De‐burn‐in technology (DBI), but it cannot be completely improved due to deviation in OLED life characteristics. In addition, managing variations in the life characteristics mentioned above is required to ensure that DBI performance is sufficient. To solve this problem, we propose a method of DBI design based on variability. By performing a short life evaluation and measuring the initial optical characteristics of each panel during the manufacturing stage, DBI settings were implemented individually. This allows for a wide range of characteristic to be resolved. In fact, we constructed a manufacturing method, and through the introduction of the architecture, the difference in brightness due to deterioration was reduced to less than 1/3.

sources.title: Bimolecular Annihilation Processes in OLEDs
sources.abstract: This thesis investigates the physical limitations and efficiency roll-off of organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) at high brightness levels. Due to the low dielectric constant of organic semiconductors, tightly bound excitons are formed, which at high current densities trigger bimolecular loss mechanisms such as triplet–triplet annihilation (TTA) and triplet–polaron annihilation (TPA). These phenomena reduce device efficiency and generate heat as well as high-energy excited states, which cause chemical damage to the materials and shorten the operational lifespan of the device. The study demonstrates that these losses can be managed by restricting exciton diffusion through host–guest systems or by accelerating radiative recombination using optical microcavities. The development of OLED devices requires a constant balance between high efficiency, durability, and manufacturing complexity. Future research should focus particularly on improving the stability of blue emitters and developing more precise kinetic models to ensure the reliability of mass-produced devices.

sources.title: Recent research on the status and advances of OLED
sources.abstract: Organic Light-Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) have already been a prominent display technology in various applications for many decades, ranging from smartphones and televisions to wearable devices and lighting. It is important to understand the current state of OLED research in order to assess its progress, identify challenges, and explore more potential ways for further development. In this paper, the significance and widespread adoption of OLED technology are briefly introduced, and its advantages over traditional display technologies are highlighted. The paper then provides a concise overview of the major components and working principles of OLEDs without delving into basic notions. The paper discusses both small molecule OLEDs (SMOLEDs) and polymer OLEDs (POLEDs), emphasizing their unique structure, characteristics and properties. Different strategies employed to enhance OLED performance is investigated, including the regulation of band gaps that influence the efficiency and brightness. This paper also focuses on the evaluation of device reliability and stability aspects. The techniques and materials employed in studies related to OLED development are also discussed with many searched experimental data and ongoing research activities. Furthermore, the research content covered the aspects of recent commercial advancements in OLED technology, such as Active matrix OLEDs (AMOLED) and Passive matrix (PMOLED). The review provides a guideline for researchers, industry professionals, and enthusiasts to better understand the OLED technology into its details, potential, and the areas that require further exploration.

sources.title: 46.1: Invited Paper: LCD Innovations vs. OLED Performance for Automotive Applications
sources.venue: SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers
sources.abstract: LCDs are today's workhorse for automotive displays. In recent years, some premium OEMs started to ship cars with OLED displays. The advantages of OLEDs compared to LCDs are short response time at low temperature (relevant for e‐mirrors) and perfect black at night as well as highly curved and transparent versions. Replacing edge‐lit backlight of LCDs by FALD (full array local dimming) results in highest luminance at acceptable halo. Furthermore, LCDs have a large supply chain, which results in competitive cost. Well‐known challenges of OLEDs deal with high luminance and temperature sensitivity, which can result in reduced lifetime (LT) incl. Burn‐In. Challenges and solutions for LCDs and OLEDs such as halo measurements and viewing angle performance will be discussed more in detail. Latest automotive demonstrators show the potential of micro‐LEDs and electrically pumped Quantum Dots (QD) displays. Both have the potential to outperform LCDs and OLEDs.

sources.title: Hyperphosphorescent OLEDs: Harnessing the Power of MR‐TADF Terminal Emitters
sources.abstract: Abstract Hyperphosphorescent organic light‐emitting diodes (HP‐OLEDs) represent an attractive solution to persistent efficiency roll‐off and device stability issues, combining phosphorescent sensitizers with fluorescent terminal emitters to achieve efficient, narrowband emission. This review discusses advances in HP‐OLEDs where the terminal emitter is a multiresonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence compound. Recent breakthroughs in device performance, including examples demonstrating both high maximum external quantum efficiencies (EQE max ) and excellent color purity, are highlighted. This review summarizes design strategies, challenges, and future directions for improving the efficiency, stability, and spectral performance of HP‐OLEDs.

sources.title: Research Progress on the Preparation of OLED Based on the Inkjet Printing
sources.abstract: Abstract Over the past few decades, organic light‐emitting diodes (OLEDs) have demonstrated compelling technological advantages due to their ability to directly convert electrons into photons without requiring backlighting, thereby offering self‐emissive surfaces, ultrathin device profiles, compatibility with flexible substrates, high luminance, and exceptional contrast ratios (achieving true black). Today, OLEDs dominate the market for small‐scale displays such as smartphones and laptops. Propelled by the burgeoning ubiquity of the Internet of Things, OLEDs are poised to experience an exponential upsurge in prospective exigency. However, conventional thermal evaporation techniques face challenges in achieving uniform large‐area OLED fabrication, rendering mass production costly and complex—a persistent drawback hindering OLEDs from becoming the undisputed market leader. Amidst this milieu, inkjet printing (IJP) has magnetized considerable scholarly and commercial traction across the panoply of fabrication modalities, crystallizing as the pre‐eminent candidate for scalable, large‐area OLED manufacturing. This technique boasts non‐contact processing, high material utilization, and compatibility with roll‐to‐roll manufacturing. In this review, the critical parameters governing ink formulation are delineated and provide an overview of prevailing OLED device architectures. Subsequently, recent advancements are consolidate in inkjet‐printed OLED layers, culminating in a circumspect prognosis of the extant impediments and the prospective trajectory toward wholly inkjet‐patterned OLED architectures.

sources.title: The Effect of Molecular Structure on the Properties of Fluorene Derivatives for OLED Applications
sources.abstract: A new family of symmetrical fluorene derivatives with different types of substituents attached to the C-2 and C-7 positions of the fluorene core synthesized by the Sonogashira coupling reactions is reported. The electronic structures and the properties of the compounds investigated by means of photoelectron emission spectroscopy, UV-Vis absorption and photoluminescent spectroscopy as well as by DFT and TD-DFT theoretical calculations are discussed. It is shown that the nature of substituents influences the π-conjugation of the molecules. No intermolecular charge transfer within the investigated wavelength range is observed. The applicability of the synthesized compounds in organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) based on exciplex emission is demonstrated. The advanced co-deposition technique with the tuned OLED architecture was applied and resulted in improved OLED parameters.

For lower photon energies or particle beams, larger perturbations may occur, necessitating further measurements or beam entry avoidance.

sources.title: Vacuum Thermal Evaporation for OLEDs: Fundamentals, Optimization, and Implications for Perovskite LEDs
sources.abstract: Abstract Organic light‐emitting diodes (OLEDs) are central to high‐end displays and solid‐state lighting due to their small thickness and high flexibility, wide color gamut, and low power consumption. While solution processing offers simplicity and cost advantages for polymer‐based OLEDs, vacuum thermal evaporation (VTE) remains the dominant method for the commercial production of high‐performance small‐molecule OLEDs, owing to its precise control over film thickness, material purity, and multilayer integration. However, to meet the demands of display applications for higher performance, lower cost and more diverse forms (such as flexibility and high resolution), it is crucial to continuously optimize the VTE process. Meanwhile, although solution processing remains the predominant approach for perovskite light‐emitting diodes (PeLEDs), recent exploratory efforts have investigated VTE as an alternative route, thereby opening opportunities to transfer process insights from OLEDs to PeLEDs. This review aims to systematically summarize the application foundation and optimization strategies of VTE technology in OLEDs, and to explore how these mature practices can inform the process development and device design of vacuum‐evaporated PeLEDs.

findings.claim: OLED lifetime and image retention (burn-in) remain a documented reliability problem, including in new manufacturing routes. Inkjet-printed OLED work still needs per-panel compensation because lifetime characteristics vary between panels.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Three abstracts converge: the SID 2026 paper says De-burn-in 'cannot be completely improved due to deviation in OLED life characteristics'. The automotive paper lists burn-in and lifetime as well-known challenges. The VR paper models burn-in as a failure mode. All three are conference abstracts and the evidence is indirect. The compensation result (brightness difference reduced to under 1/3) is a vendor-style mitigation, not a removal of the problem. No field-failure data are given.

findings.claim: Efficiency roll-off and bimolecular annihilation (TTA, TPA) at high brightness cause heat and chemical damage that shorten OLED lifespan. Blue-emitter stability is named as the key unresolved problem for reliable mass production.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: The thesis is a single non-peer-reviewed dissertation abstract. The HP-OLED review also frames roll-off and stability as 'persistent' issues, which corroborates the point. Neither provides quantitative lifetime figures in the abstract.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Future research should focus particularly on improving the stability of blue emitters and developing more precise kinetic models to ensure the reliability of mass-produced devices.

findings.claim: Large-area, low-cost manufacturing remains a barrier. Thermal evaporation is described as costly and complex for uniform large-area panels. Inkjet printing is promoted as the alternative but is still in a research and development stage, with open issues such as ink formulation and image sticking.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The inkjet review states that conventional thermal evaporation 'face[s] challenges in achieving uniform large-area OLED fabrication'. The VTE review says VTE remains dominant for high-performance small-molecule devices. This implies the incumbent process is entrenched and the printed route is not yet displacing it. The abstracts give no yield or cost data. The inkjet review's promotional wording ('pre-eminent candidate') is not backed by quantitative evidence in the abstract.

findings.claim: Competing display technologies may outperform OLED in demanding segments. For automotive use, advanced LCDs with local dimming have a large supply chain and competitive cost. Micro-LED and electrically pumped QD displays are said to have potential to outperform both LCD and OLED.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: One invited conference abstract, qualitative and 'potential' language only. No comparative cost, lifetime or yield data. Timing is not stated, so the horizon is a loose guess.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Latest automotive demonstrators show the potential of micro-LEDs and electrically pumped Quantum Dots (QD) displays. Both have the potential to outperform LCDs and OLEDs.
findings.guard_note: downgraded from verified_fact: supporting excerpt missing or not found in the cited source text

findings.claim: OLEDs are described as sensitive to high luminance and temperature, which limits their fit for harsh environments such as automotive displays.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single abstract with no quantitative thresholds.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Well‐known challenges of OLEDs deal with high luminance and temperature sensitivity, which can result in reduced lifetime (LT) incl. Burn‐In.

findings.claim: VR microdisplay burn-in results rest on simulation using a stretched exponential decay model and surrogate image content with head-motion data from a user study. The 4x slower failure under head motion is conditional on 'conservative' assumptions and is not measured device lifetime.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract reports a simulation. The user-study sample size is unstated. Surrogate content was defined by the authors. The paper shows burn-in is a recognised risk for VR OLED microdisplays and that results depend heavily on content, which makes generalisation uncertain. It also gives no direct validation against physical panels.

findings.claim: Several results are early-stage or narrow and do not show display-relevant performance. The electrically pumped organic laser is a laboratory demonstration. The fluorene derivative study shows 'improved OLED parameters' without quantified results in the abstract.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The Nature abstract notes that electrically driven organic lasers are 'very challenging' and that the device is a first demonstration. The fluorene paper reports no efficiency or lifetime numbers in the abstract. These are not display failures. They show that some of the OLED research literature gives limited commercial evidence.

findings.claim: The radiotherapy 'treat-through' OLED screen study shows measurable dose perturbation, including a 7.04% surface dose increase, and was tested on a single configuration. It is a niche medical use and is not evidence of mass-market OLED demand.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: This is an arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract reports small attenuation differences but a notable surface dose increase. The abstract is truncated. The radiation tolerance test covered 100 Gy and 12 months in a linac vault, which is limited.

hype_flags: 'Exponential upsurge in prospective exigency' for OLED demand (inkjet review): promotional language with no quantitative market evidence in the abstract.
Inkjet printing as the 'pre-eminent candidate' for scalable OLED manufacturing: the abstract gives no yield, cost or throughput data.
Micro-LED and electrically pumped QD displays 'have the potential to outperform' OLED: speculative and unquantified.
Electrically pumped organic laser: a laboratory proof of concept that should not be read as near-term commercial relevance to displays.
Burn-in compensation algorithms presented as a fix: the abstract itself says they cannot fully resolve lifetime variation.

finding.claim: S2 presents the claim that deep blue PHOLED lifetimes are 'approaching' green analogues as a verified fact. It comes from a single perspective article's own summary of progress. 'Approaching' does not mean parity, and the abstract gives no lifetime figures, conditions or luminance levels. The same abstract warns that lifetime measurement in the literature is unreliable. Other retrieved papers still name blue-emitter stability as the key unresolved problem for mass production. S1 and S2 therefore sit in tension, and S2 is stated more firmly than the evidence allows.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract itself flags measurement problems with operational lifetime. Combined with src_8078af2390, which says blue-emitter stability still needs improving for mass-produced reliability, the 'approaching green' claim should be downgraded from verified fact to an author-reported claim with caveats. The abstract does not say whether lifetimes meet commercial standards.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We also address some persistent problems commonly found in the literature concerning the measurement of quantum efficiency and operational lifetime.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S5 credits the 31% VR display power saving to exploiting the chromatic adaptation time course. The abstract attributes 31% to the combination of this technique with prior luminance dimming, so the adaptation technique's own contribution is not isolated. The result comes from one arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed). 'No statistical loss of perceptual quality' is a null result from a psychophysical study whose sample size and power are not visible in the abstract.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The quoted sentence makes the 31% figure conditional on combining with luminance dimming. The finding drops that condition. A non-significant result is not proof of no perceptual loss, and no study size is given.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Our technique can also be combined with prior work on luminance dimming to reduce display power by 31% with no statistical loss of perceptual quality.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 generalises the finding that 4th-degree polynomial regression performs comparably to look-up tables and ML models. The abstract describes data from one display, a 'high refresh-rate 4-primary OLED display'. Performance on other panels, primary counts, ageing states or temperatures is untested. The finding also does not mention that the abstract gives no error metrics (e.g. colour-difference values) for 'comparable'.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The single-device dataset limits how far the conclusion about regression methods, and the non-additivity of multi-primary OLED responses, can be extended. Quantitative margins are not available in the abstract.
finding.supporting_excerpt: we collected a large dataset of display color measurements for a high refresh-rate 4-primary OLED display.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S9 summarises the radiotherapy 'treat-through' OLED study favourably (about 0.3% mean attenuation, 100 Gy tolerance, 12 months in a vault). It omits the less favourable results in the same abstract: a 3% maximum point attenuation, a 7.04% surface dose increase, and a large spread in attenuation. It also leaves out that this is an arXiv preprint of a single screen configuration. The summary therefore understates the dosimetric trade-offs.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The 7.04% surface increase and the 3% maximum attenuation are in the abstract but absent from S9. The 12-month and 100 Gy tolerance claim comes from a single unit, so it says little about reliability across devices.
finding.supporting_excerpt: a 7.04 \% increase at the surface under an anterior-posterior beam
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S11 says OLEDs are 'appearing as form-factor enablers' and cites a spacecraft-window transparent-OLED installation. That installation is only a design concept. The study's validation was with 84 terrestrial proxy participants and 6 HCI experts, and its VR prototype did not use OLED hardware. Nothing in the abstract tests transparent-OLED performance, so the 'technically feasible' claim is the authors' own assertion. This is thin support for a trend statement about OLED form-factor use.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The abstract describes a concept plus an HCI evaluation. It does not demonstrate transparent OLED hardware in a spacecraft or give any display-technology evidence. The cited robot paper is also a generic use of an OLED component.
finding.supporting_excerpt: a future-oriented installation concept integrating transparent OLED displays with spaceship windows for real-time Earth connectivity

finding.claim: The findings leave out the main reliability, manufacturing and competition risks. S6 and S7 describe OLED as dominant and gaining traction, but no finding covers burn-in and image-sticking variation between panels (even in inkjet-printed OLEDs), high luminance and temperature sensitivity, or competing LCD, micro-LED and QD technologies. These evidence gaps weaken the optimistic framing. S6 also rests on a two-sentence abstract with no data supporting 'gaining traction'.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: src_125ddf53dd and src_f11da0f8c8 document lifetime and burn-in problems and competing technologies. A balanced picture of the market and technology status should state these limits next to the adoption claims in S6. The micro-LED and QD outperformance remark in src_125ddf53dd is itself unquantified.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Well‐known challenges of OLEDs deal with high luminance and temperature sensitivity, which can result in reduced lifetime (LT) incl. Burn‐In.

limitations: Analysis is based on 12 abstracts only. No full text was read, and several abstracts are truncated.
Few papers contain quantitative lifetime, yield, cost or market-share data, so risk magnitude cannot be assessed.
Several items are reviews, conference abstracts, a thesis or a preprint, which are not equivalent to peer-reviewed primary evidence. The arXiv radiotherapy item is a preprint.
Some papers are off-topic for display investment risk (organic laser, radiotherapy screen, fluorene chemistry).
No papers address supply chain concentration, materials supply (for example iridium or blue emitter IP), or direct comparisons with micro-LED cost, so these are gaps rather than findings.
Search coverage is limited, and absence of evidence on other risks should not be read as absence of risk.
Only titles and abstracts were available, so no full-text methods, sample sizes or quantitative margins could be checked.
Several abstracts (src_45ea9a55c9, src_b094c4dd8d) are one or two sentences long, which limits how far any claim can be tested.
Many sources are arXiv preprints or conference abstracts with no peer-review information.
S7, S8, S10 and S12 were left unchallenged because they are accurately described and already caveated.
The review covers only the 23 retrieved papers, so contradicting literature outside this set is not assessed.

draft.summary: The evidence shows OLED as an already-shipping display technology with a broad, multi-layer supply chain: SEC filings name materials and IP (Universal Display), glass substrates (Corning), photomasks (Photronics), deposition equipment (Applied Materials), display drivers (Himax), and end products in AR/wearables (Kopin, Vuzix) and automotive (Samsung Display via Dolby) [M1][M2][M3][M4][M5][M6][M7][M8][M10]. Research activity on the exact phrase 'oled displays' is rising, from 320 works in 2024 to 420 in 2025 (up 31.2%) and 322 to 515 in the same period of the current year, but the count is not normalised for overall publishing growth and many retrieved papers use OLED only as an ordinary component in unrelated systems [S12]. The clearest unresolved technical issue is blue phosphorescent emitter stability, described as a two-decade bottleneck even as one perspective claims deep-blue lifetimes are 'approaching' green analogues without lifetime figures or conditions — a claim the Risk agent challenges as stated more firmly than the evidence allows [S1][S2][C1][R2]. Reliability evidence also points to burn-in and panel-to-panel lifetime variation, including in inkjet-printed OLED, and manufacturing of large uniform panels via thermal evaporation remains costly and complex [R1][R3]. The main uncertainty is that the bullish framing rests on short abstracts and filing language, not on measured lifetime, yield or customer-volume data, and there is no patent evidence and no social/catalyst evidence in this run.
draft.plain_summary: OLED displays are the light-emitting screens used in many premium phones, some televisions, smart glasses and car dashboards, and companies already sell the materials, glass, masks and machines that go into them. The evidence suggests the technology is well established rather than brand new, but makers still struggle with blue light-emitting materials that fade too fast and with screens that can show permanent ghost images. The one thing that could hold the field back is whether those lifetime and manufacturing problems can be solved at large panel sizes and low enough cost.

themes.name: OLED manufacturing materials and equipment supply chain

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Filings show incumbent suppliers already recognising OLED revenue today: Universal Display licenses materials and IP [M1], Himax derives most revenue from TFT-LCD and OLED drivers [M2], Applied Materials sells display manufacturing equipment [M3], Corning supplies glass for LCD and OLED [M4] and Photronics supplies AMOLED/LTPS photomasks [M5]. The near term is therefore about existing order patterns in a cyclical industry rather than a new technology ramp; no finding quantifies OLED-specific revenue or capacity additions.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Whether printed OLED moves from R&D toward production is the main medium-term swing factor for the equipment and materials layer, but the findings describe inkjet printing as still requiring per-panel compensation and facing open ink-formulation and image-sticking issues [R1][R3]. No finding gives yields, volumes or capex figures, so the medium-term direction cannot be sized from this evidence.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The evidence does not support any specific long-term supply-chain forecast; it only supports that a multi-layer chain exists across materials, glass, masks, equipment and drivers [M10]. Long-run outcomes depend on large-area uniformity and cost, which the cited findings leave open [R3].

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: A complete, documented supply chain already serves OLED production, from emissive materials and patent licensing through glass, photomasks and deposition equipment to drivers and end panels [M1][M2][M3][M4][M5][M10]. Universal Display states OLED displays are capturing a growing share of the display market across phones, TVs, wearables, AR/VR and automotive [M1], and Dolby's filing indicates Samsung Display is pre-tuning OLED displays for automotive [M8], which would pull more material and equipment volume through the chain.

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: OLED remains a mainstream premium display technology with incumbent suppliers, but the cited evidence is filing-level and abstract-level. No finding provides OLED segment revenue, unit volumes or margin data for any supplier, and Himax describes the panel industry as cyclical and intensely competitive [M2]. Competing LCD, micro-LED and QD approaches are also flagged as potential outperformers, though only in an unverified claim [R4].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: Large-area, low-cost manufacturing stays a barrier: thermal evaporation is described as costly and complex for uniform large panels and inkjet printing is still in R&D with ink-formulation and image-sticking problems [R3]. Burn-in and panel-to-panel lifetime variation persist even in printed routes [R1], and OLED is described as sensitive to high luminance and temperature, limiting fit for harsh environments such as automotive [R5], where advanced LCD with local dimming has a large supply chain and competitive cost [R4].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Evidence of inkjet-printed OLED reaching production with solved ink-formulation and image-sticking issues would strengthen the manufacturing case; the findings currently show it at R&D stage [R3].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Disclosed OLED-specific revenue or capacity additions from materials, equipment, glass, mask or driver suppliers would confirm the demand path implied by filings, which today only show segment-level involvement [M1][M2][M3][M4][M5].

catalysts.label: forecast

risks.label: ai_interpretation

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: Optimistic framing of OLED dominance and traction [S6][S7] sits against reliability, manufacturing and competition points absent from those findings: burn-in and panel variation [R1], costly and complex large-area evaporation with printing still in R&D [R3], sensitivity to high luminance and temperature in automotive [R5], and LCD/micro-LED/QD competition (unverified claim) [R4][C6].

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The findings provide no timeline or commercial milestone for blue PHOLED adoption; they only state that 100% internal efficiency phosphorescent emitters have not met required stability standards for over two decades [S1]. No near-term conclusion is supported.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: One perspective reports deep-blue PHOLED lifetimes approaching green analogues through combined molecular design, graded doping, increased optical density of states and outcoupling [S2], but the Risk challenge notes this is a single perspective article's summary with no lifetime figures, conditions or luminance levels, and that literature lifetime measurement is described as unreliable [C1]. A separate finding still names blue-emitter stability the key unresolved problem for reliable mass production [R2], so the medium term is genuinely contested.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The evidence does not support a long-term claim either way. Blue emitters consume roughly half the energy of an OLED front plane, which explains the incentive [S1], but efficiency roll-off and bimolecular annihilation at high brightness are cited as mechanisms that shorten lifespan and would have to be managed [R2].

bull.label: ai_interpretation
bull.narrative: Blue pixels use roughly half the energy of an OLED display front plane, so solving blue emitter stability would matter materially for power and lifetime [S1]. Progress is reported from combined molecular design, graded doping of the emission layer, increased optical density of states to shorten triplet radiative lifetime, and light outcoupling schemes, with deep-blue lifetimes claimed to be approaching green analogues [S2].

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: Blue emitter stability has been a bottleneck for over two decades and 100% internal efficiency phosphorescent emitters have not met adoption stability standards [S1], while a separate paper still calls blue-emitter stability the key unresolved problem for reliable mass production [R2]. The claimed progress toward green-like lifetimes is an unquantified summary in a single perspective article whose own abstract warns that lifetime measurement is unreliable [S2][C1].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The improvement claim is 'approaching', not parity, and comes with no lifetime figures, conditions or luminance levels [C1]. Efficiency roll-off and bimolecular annihilation at high brightness cause heat and chemical damage that shorten lifespan [R2], and lifetime and image-retention problems are still documented in current manufacturing routes [R1]. On this evidence the bottleneck may persist well beyond the stated horizon.

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Publication of peer-reviewed blue PHOLED lifetime data with measurement conditions, luminance levels and reproducibility would materially strengthen the progress case [S2][C1].

catalysts.label: assumption

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: There is product evidence but no volume or margin evidence: findings name specific products and programmes without unit shipments, revenue or design-win counts [M6][M7][M8]. VR microdisplay burn-in findings are simulation-based with conservative assumptions rather than measured lifetime [R6], and the 'gaining traction' claim is supported only by a short abstract with no data [S6][C6].

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: OLED is described as sensitive to high luminance and temperature, which limits its fit for harsh environments such as automotive displays [R5], and MicroLED is named as a competing microdisplay route with potential to outperform, with Kopin itself reporting progress toward MicroLED production by mid-2027 [R4][M6]. A spacecraft-window transparent-OLED 'installation' sometimes cited as a form-factor trend is only a design concept whose VR prototype did not use OLED hardware [C5][S11].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Named, quantified automotive design wins or production commitments beyond the Samsung Display pre-tuning indication would strengthen the adoption case [M8].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: Measured (rather than simulated) VR/microdisplay lifetime and burn-in data would strengthen confidence in wearable use [R6].

catalysts.label: forecast
catalysts.text: OLED hardware — not concepts — used in validated transparent or unusual form-factor products would support the form-factor claim now resting on a design concept [C5][S11].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Microdisplays are a small part of large diversified reported businesses, and Kopin's own medium-term roadmap points to MicroLED production by mid-2027, so OLED microdisplay exposure may shrink rather than grow [M6][M8].

risks.label: ai_interpretation
risks.text: Kopin shows a deep drawdown with 20-day annualised volatility of 127.8% and a 45.1% distance from its 100-day high; extreme volatility is a timing risk, not a technology signal [T1][T2].

risks.label: unverified_claim
risks.text: Competing routes (LCD with local dimming, micro-LED, electrically pumped QD) are said to have potential to outperform OLED in demanding segments, though this is an unverified claim [R4].

companies.label: ai_interpretation
companies.name: Kopin Corp
companies.relevance: Ships OLED microdisplays with OLED among funded product lines and R&D areas, while pursuing domestic MicroLED production by mid-2027 under a U.S. Army program. Small company, and timing data show severe recent drawdown and very high volatility (risk context only) [T2].

companies.label: ai_interpretation
companies.name: Vuzix Corp
companies.relevance: Ships M400 and LX1 smart glasses using OLED displays and sells waveguides that can pair with third-party display engines; also sells microLED-based Shield products, so OLED is one of several routes. No OLED unit volumes given.

companies.label: ai_interpretation
companies.name: Dolby Laboratories, Inc.
companies.relevance: Its 10-K states Samsung Display is working with Dolby to pre-tune OLED displays for automotive applications, indicating OLED penetration into automotive displays; OLED is not Dolby's own product line, so this is an ecosystem signal rather than a revenue driver.

invalidation_conditions.label: forecast
invalidation_conditions.text: Evidence that OLED microdisplay design wins are being replaced by MicroLED or other routes in AR/VR and automotive would invalidate the adoption part of this theme [M6][R4].

invalidation_conditions.label: forecast
invalidation_conditions.text: Measured lifetime and burn-in data failing automotive and wearable requirements would invalidate the wearable/automotive case [R5][R6].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: The Science finding that OLED is gaining traction in automotive, IT and AR/VR [S6] is weakened by the challenge that it rests on a two-sentence abstract with no supporting data [C6] and by the finding that OLED is temperature- and luminance-sensitive, limiting automotive fit [R5].

conflicting_evidence.label: ai_interpretation
conflicting_evidence.text: The transparent-OLED 'form-factor enabler' claim [S11] is undercut by the challenge that it is a design concept validated with terrestrial proxy participants and non-OLED VR hardware, with no test of transparent-OLED performance [C5].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Code-computed OpenAlex counts of works containing the exact phrase 'oled displays' rose from 320 in 2024 to 420 in 2025 (up 31.2%), and the same period of the current year shows 322 to 515 (up 59.9%, rising), so momentum is still building rather than fading. Caveats: the count is not normalised for overall publishing growth, synonyms are excluded, and several retrieved papers use OLED only as an ordinary component [S12].

dimension_ratings.note: no supporting finding cited, so treated as an assumption
dimension_ratings.rationale: The Patent agent did not run, so there is no patent evidence and no code-computed patent counts in this assessment. No rating can be supported.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: OLED displays demonstrably ship (dominant premium-smartphone technology, traction in automotive, IT and AR/VR [S6]; supplier and product filings [M1][M6][M7][M8]), so the base technology is feasible. However the cited improvement paths are not proven: blue phosphorescent stability has been a two-decade bottleneck [S1] and is still named the key unresolved problem for mass production [R2], and inkjet printing remains at R&D stage [R3]. Rating reflects a working technology whose frontier remains open.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Market findings show commercial products and revenue today: Universal Display sells OLED materials and licenses IP and describes OLED displays capturing a growing share across phones, TVs, wearables, AR/VR and automotive [M1]; Himax derives 80.0% of 2025 revenue from drivers used in TFT-LCD and OLED panels [M2]; Vuzix and Kopin ship OLED-based products [M6][M7]; Samsung Display pre-tunes automotive OLED with Dolby [M8]. No finding breaks out OLED-specific revenue, which caps confidence below high.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Adoption evidence is product-level rather than volume-level: Vuzix ships OLED smart glasses [M7], Kopin ships OLED microdisplays among funded lines [M6], and Samsung Display works with Dolby on automotive pre-tuning [M8]. Ostin Technology describes OLED as a potential alternative flat-panel technology that may gain wider acceptance [M9], and no finding gives unit volumes or named end-customer commitments.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Incumbent suppliers commit resources to OLED inputs: Applied Materials runs a Display segment selling LCD/OLED manufacturing equipment [M3], Photronics supplies AMOLED and LTPS photomasks [M5], Corning supplies display glass for LCD and OLED [M4], and Universal Display spends 22.5% of revenue on R&D [K1]. No finding quantifies OLED-specific capex or capacity additions, so this is involvement rather than a measured investment cycle.

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: OLED is described as the dominant premium-smartphone display technology with traction in automotive, IT and AR/VR [S6], and Universal Display characterises it as gaining share across multiple markets [M1]. Against that, Himax calls the panel industry cyclical and intensely competitive [M2], and an unverified claim says LCD with local dimming, micro-LED and electrically pumped QD displays have potential to outperform OLED in demanding segments [R4]; OLED is also called sensitive to luminance and temperature, limiting automotive fit [R5].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: The findings document a layered supply chain across materials and IP (Universal Display) [M1], glass substrates (Corning) [M4], photomasks (Photronics) [M5], manufacturing equipment (Applied Materials) [M3], drivers (Himax) [M2] and end products (Kopin, Vuzix) [M6][M7], summarised in M10. The one visible gap is that the next-generation large-area/printed route is still in R&D [R3].

dimension_ratings.label: ai_interpretation
dimension_ratings.rationale: Level 3 (elevated): OLED products ship with real customers and a documented supply chain [M1][M6][M7][M8][M10], but scaling and reliability are still unproven — blue-emitter stability remains the key unresolved issue for mass production [R2], burn-in and panel-to-panel lifetime variation persist [R1], large-area low-cost manufacturing is a barrier with printing at R&D stage [R3], and OLED is temperature/luminance-sensitive [R5]. Timing adds risk: Kopin is in a deep drawdown with 127.8% 20-day annualised volatility [T1][T2], though Apple shows no stretch signal [T3][T5]. It is not level 4 because the technology is clearly shipping with paying customers, and not 2 because core technical and manufacturing questions remain open.

No news headlines at all were supplied; no third-party industry analysis, no pricing/panel-cost data, and no evidence on panel-maker capex plans.
Price/timing evidence covers only two OLED-linked tickers (Kopin, Apple); no timing data for Universal Display, Himax, Applied Materials, Corning, Photronics or Vuzix [T1][T3][T5].
Company Scout coverage includes two very small or micro-revenue entities (Fabric.AI with 2 filings and -87.2% growth, Ostin with 1 filing) where the topic mention may be incidental [K2][K3].
limitations: Only Science, Risk, Market, Price/Timing and Company Scout evidence is available; the Patent and X agents did not run, so patent momentum is unrated and there is no catalyst/news layer.
Several Science findings are two-sentence abstracts, low-confidence (S8, S10, S11) or unquantified, and the Risk challenges C1-C6 weaken or reframe S2, S4, S5, S9, S11, S6 and S7 specifically.

Research-activity metrics count only the exact phrase 'oled displays', exclude synonyms and abbreviations, are not normalised for overall publishing growth, and include papers that use OLED merely as a component in unrelated systems [S12].

Company Scout next-runner scores are code-computed heuristics derived from filings, not predictions of returns or of commercial success, and small companies named there carry higher risk and less disclosure.
Price and timing findings are ~100-trading-day, rule-based metrics; they are risk context only and must not be read as entry points, timing signals or price expectations.

Ratings are constrained by rule 6: market dimensions are rated only from company filings and direct market findings, so they describe what companies report, not independently verified market share or demand.
No marketing, teardown, supply-agreement, pricing or production-yield data is available, so commercial and supply-chain ratings rest on filing language rather than measured output.
